items.prompt: A team wants a server-side layer that fans out to several backend services and reshapes the combined result for exactly one type of client. What's this pattern called?
items.explanation: A BFF is defined by exactly this: a thin layer, specific to one client type, that calls several backend services and combines/reshapes their responses into what that one client needs.
items.reference:
Mobile BFF

combines price+stock+reviews for one cellular round trip

Web BFF

combines the same data, shaped differently

Why: one BFF per client type is what lets each get exactly the shape it needs, without a shared endpoint negotiating between them.
items.reflection: Think of another two-sided mismatch you've dealt with outside software -- two audiences wanting the same core content shaped differently (a conference talk recorded live and also packaged for video-on-demand, say). What's the 'shared endpoint' you'd be tempted to force into one shape, and what would a BFF-style split look like there?

items.prompt: Which best describes what a Backend for Frontend (BFF) does?
choices: A client-agnostic layer handling auth and routing for every client
Aggregates and reshapes backend responses for one specific frontend
A read-replica database used for scaling reads
A CDN edge cache for static assets
items.explanation: Aggregation and client-specific reshaping is the BFF's whole job. Auth/routing for every client is the API gateway's job, not the BFF's.

Mobile BFF → owned near the mobile team. Web BFF → owned near the web team. Gateway → owned by platform/infra.

items.prompt: A shared REST API returns one resource per endpoint. A mobile screen that needs 4 resources, without a BFF, has to make how many sequential round trips before it can render?
items.explanation: Without an aggregation layer, each resource is its own round trip -- 4 resources means 4 separate requests before the screen has everything it needs.
items.reference:
Without BFF

4 sequential calls, ~880ms

With BFF

1 call, ~220ms

Why: chattiness is literally counted in round trips -- moving the fan-out server-side is what collapses 4 into 1.
items.reflection: Chattiness isn't only an API problem -- think of a real-world process that forces many small round trips (several separate forms, several separate approvals) where one combined step would do. What would the 'BFF' for that process look like?

It reduces the number of backend services that exist, consolidating product, inventory, and reviews into one
items.explanation: The client's round trip crosses a slow, variable public network (or cellular). Once the fan-out happens inside the data center, service-to-service calls are typically much faster -- the client then only pays one slow round trip instead of several.

items.prompt: What problem does contract testing solve once a system is split into a BFF and several independently deployed domain services?
choices: It makes every service run faster, since contracts let CI skip running the provider's test suite
It lets services deploy independently while still catching breaking changes before they ship
It replaces the need for an API gateway, since contracts already enforce auth and rate limiting
It removes the need for a BFF entirely, since contracts handle aggregation across domain services
items.explanation: Splitting into independent services creates a new risk: one service's change silently breaking another. Contract testing catches that risk fast, without forcing services back into lockstep deploys.
items.reference:
Consumer (BFF) records what it needs → provider (domain service) checks its real responses against that, in its own CI, before every deploy.

Why: the whole point is catching breakage fast without forcing a slow, shared integration test.
items.reflection: Contracts that check only what's actually used, not everything that could exist, show up outside software too. Think of a handoff between two teams (design to engineering, sales to delivery) where a lightweight 'here's exactly what I need from you' agreement would replace a slower, full review.

items.explanation: That's exactly what a consumer-driven contract test is for: verify the provider's real handler against what the consumer recorded it needs, with neither service's full stack actually running.

items.prompt: Write promoField(result) for an optional promotions field, following the same rule: result is { status: 'ok', discountPercent } or any other status shape. Return { discountPercent } when status is 'ok', otherwise return { unavailable: true }.

tests.description: returns discountPercent when status is ok

items.explanation: The check is 'is it ok', not 'is it exactly unavailable' -- any non-success status (timeout, unavailable, a future new status) should degrade the same way, so the page never breaks just because a new failure mode was added upstream without every caller being updated to recognize its exact name.

return the real data

anything else

return { unavailable: true }

items.prompt: Write assertLoadBearing(product, inventory) that throws new Error('aggregation failed') if either product.status or inventory.status is 'error', and otherwise does nothing (returns undefined).

tests.description: does not throw when both succeeded

items.explanation: This isolates the 'fail the whole request' half of the per-field policy into its own guard: called before building the response, it stops load-bearing failures from ever reaching a caller as a half-built, misleadingly-successful page.
items.reference:
price and inStock are load-bearing: a product page without them isn't a worse page, it's a broken one -- so the request should fail loudly, not render.

Why: not every field can degrade gracefully -- some are worth failing the whole request over.

items.prompt: Write isOk(result) that returns true if result.status === 'ok', false otherwise.
items.explanation: Checking for the success case directly is the building block behind every degrade/throw decision in the unit's aggregation code.

items.prompt: Write unavailableMarker() that returns { unavailable: true }.
items.explanation: The exact degraded value every optional field falls back to when its upstream call didn't succeed.

items.prompt: Write failedLoadBearingError() that returns new Error('aggregation failed') (don't throw it, just return the Error object).

tests.description: returns an Error with the right message

items.explanation: This is the exact error thrown whenever a load-bearing field fails -- a stable, recognizable signal rather than a generic error.

items.prompt: Write degradeOrThrow(result, isLoadBearing) that throws new Error('aggregation failed') if isLoadBearing is true and result.status !== 'ok'; otherwise returns result.status === 'ok' ? result.data : { unavailable: true }.
items.explanation: This generalizes the per-field rule into one function: load-bearing failures throw, optional failures degrade -- exactly the explicit choice an author has to make per field.

items.prompt: Write stockField(inventory) that returns inventory.inStock when inventory.status === 'ok', assuming inventory is always load-bearing so this function never needs to degrade -- just read the field directly without any status check.
items.explanation: A load-bearing field, once its status has already been checked elsewhere, is read directly -- no degrade branch needed, unlike an optional field.

items.prompt: Write shouldDegrade(status) that returns true for any status that is NOT 'ok' (timeout, unavailable, error, anything), and false only for 'ok'.

tests.description: true for an unexpected new status

items.explanation: Checking 'not ok' rather than listing every known failure name is exactly what makes degrade logic resilient to a brand-new failure mode showing up later.

items.prompt: Write combineGuards(a, b) that throws new Error('aggregation failed') if a.status !== 'ok' OR b.status !== 'ok', and otherwise returns undefined.

tests.description: throws if a is not ok

items.explanation: A minimal two-field load-bearing guard -- the same shape as assertLoadBearing, just renamed, reinforcing that the guard logic is the same regardless of which two fields are load-bearing.

items.prompt: Write recommendationsOrEmpty(result) that returns result.items when result.status === 'ok', or an empty array [] otherwise (a different degrade value than { unavailable: true }, just to show degrading doesn't always mean the same marker shape).
items.explanation: Degrading doesn't have to mean the same { unavailable: true } marker every time -- the right degraded value depends on what the page does with that field; an empty list can render just as gracefully as an explicit marker.

items.prompt: Write totalFanoutTime(latenciesMs, mode) that computes total aggregation time for a set of upstream calls. latenciesMs is an array of numbers (one per call). If mode is 'sequential', return their sum (each call has to wait for the previous one, as in a chain of plain awaits). If mode is 'parallel', return their max (the whole fan-out is bounded by the slowest call, as with Promise.all).

tests.description: parallel mode returns the max latency
parallel mode with uneven latencies is bounded by the slowest
single call gives the same result either way

items.explanation: This is the arithmetic behind the unit's fan-out chart: sequential awaits pay the full sum of every call because each one blocks the next; Promise.all starts every call at once, so total time is set by whichever call finishes last, not by how many calls there are.
items.reference:
sequential

sum of every call's latency

parallel

bounded by the slowest call

Why: the gap between sum and max is exactly why buildProductPage above uses Promise.all instead of sequential awaits.
items.reflection: The sum-vs-max gap between sequential and parallel work isn't unique to network calls -- it shows up in any workflow where steps could run independently but get run one after another out of habit. Where have you seen that in a non-engineering process?

items.prompt: Write sumLatencies(latenciesMs) that returns the sum of all numbers in the array.
items.explanation: This is exactly the sequential half of totalFanoutTime -- each call's latency adds to the next because nothing starts until the previous one finishes.

items.prompt: Write maxLatency(latenciesMs) that returns the largest number in the array.
items.explanation: This is the parallel half of totalFanoutTime -- Promise.all bounds total time by whichever call finishes last.

items.prompt: Write isSequential(mode) that returns true if mode === 'sequential', false otherwise.
items.explanation: A small building block for branching between the two fan-out modes.

items.prompt: Write twoCallsSequential(a, b) that returns a + b, the total time for two sequential awaits with latencies a and b.
items.explanation: The simplest possible case of the sequential rule: two chained awaits take as long as both calls combined.

items.prompt: Write twoCallsParallel(a, b) that returns the larger of a and b, the total time for two calls run with Promise.all.
items.explanation: The simplest possible case of the parallel rule: two calls started together finish together with the slower one.

items.prompt: Write slowestCallIndex(latenciesMs) that returns the array index of the largest latency.

tests.description: finds the index of the slowest call

items.explanation: Knowing WHICH call is the bottleneck, not just how long it took, is useful for deciding where to focus a timeout or a performance fix.

items.prompt: Write speedupRatio(sequentialTotal, parallelTotal) that returns sequentialTotal / parallelTotal.
items.explanation: This is literally how much faster parallel fan-out is than sequential for a given set of calls -- the gap the unit's chart visualizes.

items.prompt: Write addCallToSequential(currentTotal, newCallLatency) that returns currentTotal + newCallLatency -- how adding one more sequential call changes the total.
items.explanation: Every additional sequential call adds its full latency to the running total -- this is why the sequential bars in the unit's chart grow linearly with each added service.

items.prompt: Write matchesContract(response, requiredFields) that acts like a tiny consumer-driven contract check. requiredFields is an array of [fieldName, expectedType] pairs (expectedType is a string like 'number' or 'string', checked with typeof). Return true only if response has every required field present with the matching typeof; return false otherwise. Extra fields on response that aren't in requiredFields must NOT cause a false -- a contract only checks what the consumer actually reads.

tests.description: passes when every required field matches
fails when a required field is missing
fails when a field has the wrong type
an unrelated extra field on the response does not break the contract

items.explanation: Checking only requiredFields, and ignoring anything else on response, is exactly what makes a consumer-driven contract narrow: a provider adding new fields (like topReviewIds) never breaks a consumer that never asked for them, which is what lets providers extend their API freely.
items.reference:
Contract checks: does response have averageRating (number) and reviewCount (number)? It never asks whether response has ONLY those fields.

Why: checking a subset, not an exact match, is what keeps a contract from breaking on every unrelated provider change.
items.reflection: A check that verifies only the fields it actually cares about, ignoring everything else, mirrors how a good review -- code review, spec review, contract review -- should work. Where have you seen a review get bogged down checking things nobody actually depended on?

items.prompt: Write hasField(response, field) that returns true if response[field] is not undefined.
items.explanation: Checking presence is the first half of a contract check, before even looking at the field's type.

items.prompt: Write typeMatches(value, expectedType) that returns typeof value === expectedType.
items.explanation: This is the exact comparison matchesContract runs for every required field -- typeof against the expected type string.

items.prompt: Write checkOneField(response, field, type) that returns true if typeof response[field] === type.
items.explanation: One required field, checked on its own -- matchesContract just repeats this check for every entry in requiredFields.

items.prompt: Write allFieldsPresent(response, fields) that returns true if every field name in the fields array exists on response (response[f] !== undefined for all f).
items.explanation: Checking presence across a list of fields, before checking types, is the first pass a full contract check runs.

items.prompt: Write countMismatches(response, requiredFields) that returns how many [field, type] pairs in requiredFields do NOT match (missing or wrong type).

tests.description: counts a missing field and a type mismatch

items.explanation: This is the same logic as matchesContract, just counting failures instead of stopping at the first one -- useful for reporting exactly what broke.

items.prompt: Write pickFields(response, fields) that returns a new object containing only the keys listed in fields, taken from response.
items.explanation: This mirrors the contract's own narrow focus -- extracting only the fields that matter, and leaving everything else (like an unrelated extra field) untouched and ignored.

items.prompt: Write isNumberField(response, field) that returns true if typeof response[field] === 'number'.
items.explanation: A specialized version of typeMatches for the most common contract field type in this unit's examples.

items.prompt: Write isStringField(response, field) that returns true if typeof response[field] === 'string'.
items.explanation: The string-typed counterpart to isNumberField -- the same idea, applied to a field like product name.
